lessons.title: Generate mood boards and concept directions from a creative brief with ChatGPT and Gemini
lessons.summary: Turn a short creative brief into 3-4 genuinely distinct visual directions with ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 or Gemini's native image generation, instead of one polished-but-arbitrary board.
lessons.goal: Produce 3-4 distinct, on-brief visual directions (a small mood board per direction) from a single project brief using ChatGPT or Gemini, to open a design project with client-ready options.
lessons.whyItMatters: Early concept exploration used to mean hours scouring stock sites and Pinterest for reference images that only sort-of matched the brief. ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 and Gemini's native image generation let you generate genuinely varied directions — different palettes, textures, and moods — from the same brief in the time it used to take to find one usable reference. GPT Image 2 tends to follow a detailed brief most reliably across several very different directions run in one sitting; Gemini's native generation is a strong alternative, and quicker to iterate on when a direction leans toward a graphic or infographic-style look. Clients also respond better to comparing a few clear directions than reacting to a single early design, so distinct, well-labeled directions are the real deliverable here, not one "best" image.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a ChatGPT or Gemini account open (this lesson's prompt works in either — GPT Image 2 in ChatGPT, or Gemini's native image generation) and a real or practice project brief ready.
steps: Write a one-paragraph creative brief: the project, the audience, the feeling you want, and any hard constraints (existing brand colors, a competitor to differentiate from, a material or format restriction).
Turn the brief into 3-4 deliberately different creative directions — not variations of the same idea, but genuinely distinct takes (e.g., minimal/editorial vs. warm/tactile vs. bold/graphic).
For each direction, write a separate structured prompt in ChatGPT or Gemini: subject/scene, palette, texture/material cues, lighting, and mood — reusing the brief's constraints in every one.
Generate 3-4 images per direction so each board has enough range to read as a direction, not a single lucky image.
Label each board plainly with the direction name and a one-line rationale for why it fits the brief.
Present all directions together, not sequentially — side-by-side comparison is what lets a client or team react usefully.
Note which specific prompt lines produced the reactions you want, so you can push that direction further in the next round.
lessons.prompt:
Brief: [PROJECT, AUDIENCE, DESIRED FEELING, CONSTRAINTS — e.g., existing brand colors, a competitor to differentiate from, format requirements]

Generate concept imagery for DIRECTION [1/2/3/4]: [DIRECTION NAME AND ONE-LINE DESCRIPTION, e.g., "Minimal & Editorial — restrained, high-contrast, lots of white space"]

[SUBJECT/SCENE reflecting this direction], [COMPOSITION], [COLOR PALETTE for this direction], [TEXTURE/MATERIAL CUES], [LIGHTING], [MOOD], [ASPECT RATIO/FORMAT]

Stay within the brief's constraints above. Do not include any literal text, logo, or brand mark in the image.
lessons.explanation: Writing a separate, structured prompt per direction — rather than one prompt with "or" options — is what produces boards that actually read as distinct instead of near-duplicates of the same aesthetic. This holds in both ChatGPT and Gemini, though GPT Image 2's stronger instruction-following tends to keep more of the fine detail (specific texture and lighting cues) intact across several very different directions run back-to-back, while Gemini's native generation is faster to iterate on if a direction leans toward a graphic or infographic-style look. Reusing the brief's constraints in every direction keeps all the boards eligible for approval; a direction that ignores an existing brand color isn't a real option, it's a distraction. Generating a small set of images per direction, rather than one image, matters because a single generation can be a lucky outlier — three or four images make it clear whether a direction actually holds together.
lessons.example:
Brief: a rebrand for a boutique neighborhood bakery, audience is young professionals who value quality over convenience, desired feeling is "craft, not corporate," existing brand color is a deep terracotta.

Expected output: three labeled boards — "Minimal & Editorial" (terracotta as a single accent against cream and charcoal, clean product shots, generous negative space), "Warm & Tactile" (terracotta paired with flour-dust textures, natural wood, soft window light), and "Bold & Graphic" (terracotta as a dominant field color, thick illustrated linework, high contrast) — each with 3-4 images and a one-line rationale, all clearly using the same terracotta constraint in a different way.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini, write a real brief for a project you're starting (or a personal project) and generate 3 distinct directions with 3-4 images each, labeled and ready to compare side by side.
lessons.expectedResult: Three to four clearly distinct, labeled mood boards from one brief, ready to present together, each internally consistent enough to read as a direction rather than a single lucky image.
commonMistakes: Generating variations of one idea and calling them "different directions" — a client can't meaningfully choose between near-duplicates.
Skipping the written rationale, so nobody remembers why a direction was included by the time of the review meeting.
Not enforcing brand constraints (like an existing palette) in every direction, producing boards that get rejected on sight.
Presenting boards one at a time instead of together, which anchors reactions to whichever one is shown first.
lessons.proTip: Keep the constraints paragraph identical, word for word, across all direction prompts and only vary the direction-specific lines — that discipline is what makes the boards genuinely comparable instead of accidentally biased by inconsistent wording. Stick to one tool (ChatGPT or Gemini) for a single brief's full set of directions, since switching mid-brief can introduce its own style drift.

lessons.title: Turn a vague client ask into a clear creative brief with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn a few rough lines from a client into a structured brief with the right questions flagged, before spending a single hour designing against a guess.
lessons.goal: Convert a vague client request into a structured creative brief plus a short list of specific clarifying questions, before any design work starts.
lessons.whyItMatters: The single biggest cause of wasted design time is starting work from an ambiguous ask — "make it pop," "something modern," "like our competitor but different." A structured intake pass that separates what's actually known from what's still assumed saves rounds of revisions later, and asking sharp, specific clarifying questions up front reads as competence to most clients, not friction.
steps: Paste the client's raw message or call notes exactly as received, however vague or informal.
Use the brief-intake prompt, which asks Claude to separate stated facts from assumptions rather than guess at either.
Review the "Assumptions to confirm" list and remove anything you already know the answer to from prior context.
Send the clarifying questions to the client before starting any visual work, not alongside a first draft.
Once answers come back, paste them in and ask Claude to fold them into a final one-page brief.
Save the final brief in your project file as the reference point for any later scope discussion.
lessons.prompt:
I'm turning a client request into a design brief. Here is the client's raw message/notes:
[PASTE CLIENT MESSAGE OR CALL NOTES]

Do the following:
1. List only what is explicitly stated as a fact or requirement (project type, audience, deadline, budget, format, any concrete preference mentioned).
2. List everything that would normally belong in a brief but is missing or ambiguous, under "Assumptions to confirm" — do not guess at an answer, phrase each as a specific question I can send the client (e.g., not "what's the budget" but "is the budget range still $X-Y from our call, or has that changed?").
3. Flag any vague stylistic language in the request (e.g., "modern," "pop," "clean") and suggest 2-3 concrete reference directions I could show the client to pin down what they actually mean.

Do not invent a project scope, timeline, or requirement that wasn't stated or implied.
lessons.explanation: Separating stated facts from assumptions is what stops a brief from quietly hardening a guess into a requirement — the two-list structure forces every unclear point into a question you actually send, rather than a decision you make silently on the client's behalf. Turning vague style words into concrete reference directions works because "modern" means something different to every client; showing 2-3 options gets you a real answer in one message instead of a rejected first draft weeks later. Banning invented scope or timeline keeps the brief honest about what you actually know right now.
lessons.example:
Client message: "Hey can you refresh our logo, make it feel more modern? Need it soon-ish."

Expected output: facts confirmed — "refresh of an existing logo requested"; assumptions to confirm — "By 'soon-ish,' is there a specific deadline, such as an upcoming launch or event?", "Is there a budget range already agreed for this project?", "Should the color palette and mark stay recognizable as an evolution, or is a full departure open for consideration?"; and 2-3 concrete visual reference directions to show the client to pin down what "modern" means to them specifically.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, take a real (or recent) vague client request and run it through this prompt, then actually send the resulting questions before starting any design work.
lessons.expectedResult: A one-page brief split into confirmed facts and open questions, plus specific clarifying questions ready to send — with nothing about scope, timeline, or style invented.
commonMistakes: Starting design work before sending the clarifying questions, which just relocates the guesswork instead of removing it.
Asking broad, unanswerable questions ("what's your budget?") instead of the specific, easy-to-answer phrasing the prompt produces.
Treating the first brief as final instead of updating it once the client answers.
Letting Claude guess at a budget or timeline range instead of flagging it as unknown.
lessons.proTip: Keep the finished, client-confirmed brief as the reference you point back to if scope creeps mid-project — it's far easier to say "this wasn't in the brief we agreed on" than to relitigate a memory of a phone call.

lessons.title: Draft UX copy and microcopy for a screen or flow with Claude
lessons.summary: Generate first-draft button labels, empty states, error messages, and onboarding copy that match your product's voice and actually help the user know what to do next.
lessons.goal: Produce a full set of UX copy for one screen or flow — headline, body, button labels, error and empty states — consistent in voice and grounded in the real interaction.
lessons.whyItMatters: Microcopy is disproportionately high-leverage — a confusing error message or a vague button label creates support tickets and drop-off that no visual redesign fixes. Designers are increasingly asked to draft this copy themselves rather than wait on a copywriter for every screen, but generic AI-written copy reads exactly like generic AI-written copy unless you constrain it to the actual interaction and a defined voice.
steps: Describe the screen or flow precisely: what the user is trying to do, what state they're in, and what happens after each possible action.
Define (or paste) your product's voice in 3-5 adjectives with one example sentence, so the copy isn't generic.
Use the microcopy prompt to generate every piece of text the screen needs in one pass — not just the obvious headline.
Explicitly request error and empty states, which are the pieces designers most often forget to write until QA.
Read every button label out loud in context — does it describe the action, not just repeat the screen title?
Trim anything over the character limits your UI actually allows.
Hand the approved copy to whoever owns final content review before shipping, if that isn't you.
lessons.prompt:
I need UX copy for one screen/flow in a product. Voice: [3-5 ADJECTIVES, e.g., "direct, warm, no jargon"], example of our voice: "[PASTE ONE EXAMPLE SENTENCE FROM EXISTING PRODUCT COPY]".

Screen/flow description: [DESCRIBE: what the user is trying to do, what triggered this screen, what happens on each possible action]

Write:
1. Headline (under [X] characters)
2. Supporting body text (1-2 sentences)
3. Primary and secondary button labels (verb-first, describing the actual action, under [X] characters each)
4. Empty state copy (if this screen can have nothing to show)
5. Error state copy for the most likely failure (be specific about what went wrong and what to do next, not "Something went wrong")
6. Any tooltip or helper text needed to clarify a non-obvious control

Match the voice above exactly. Do not invent a feature, limit, or behavior the screen doesn't actually have.
lessons.explanation: Asking for every piece of text a screen needs in one pass — not just the headline — is what surfaces the error and empty states designers routinely forget until a bug report exposes the gap. Requiring verb-first button labels tied to the actual action, rather than a repeat of the screen title ("Continue" everywhere), is what makes a flow scannable instead of ambiguous under time pressure. Providing a voice definition with one real example sentence keeps the draft from defaulting to generic SaaS copy, since the model has an actual reference to match rather than an abstract adjective list.
lessons.example:
Screen: connecting a bank account during onboarding in a budgeting app. Voice: "direct, reassuring, no jargon," example sentence: "We'll only ever show you your own numbers."

Expected output includes a headline like "Connect your bank to see where your money goes," a primary button labeled "Connect my bank" (not "Continue"), an error state for a failed connection that says what happened and what to try next rather than "Something went wrong," and an empty state for before any account is connected that reassures rather than nags.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, describe one real screen or flow from a current project, define its voice, and generate the full copy set with this prompt.
lessons.expectedResult: A complete first-draft copy set for one screen — headline, body, buttons, empty state, error state, and any needed tooltip — in a consistent, defined voice, ready for review rather than a bare headline and placeholder buttons.
commonMistakes: Only asking for the headline and body, then writing button labels and error states as an afterthought.
Skipping the voice definition, which produces copy that sounds like every other product's default tone.
Accepting a vague error message ("Something went wrong") instead of pushing for what happened and what to do next.
Not checking character counts against the actual UI component before handing copy to engineering.
lessons.proTip: Save your voice definition and one example sentence as a reusable snippet — reusing the exact wording every time keeps copy consistent across screens written weeks apart.

lessons.title: Write a design rationale document and presentation talking points with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn your design decisions into a clear rationale document and spoken presentation notes that hold up under stakeholder pushback.
lessons.goal: Produce a design rationale document plus condensed spoken presentation notes that connect each major decision back to a real constraint, user need, or brief requirement.
lessons.whyItMatters: Designers lose arguments they should win because the rationale lives only in their head — a stakeholder asks "why not just make the button bigger" and the answer gets improvised on the spot instead of already being documented. A written rationale, prepared before the meeting, turns a design review from a taste debate into a decision review, and speaking from prepared talking points rather than reading slide text keeps the actual presentation confident.
steps: List your actual decisions and the real reason behind each one — a brief requirement, a research finding, a technical constraint, an accessibility requirement, or a brand guideline. Don't include a decision you can't actually justify.
Use the rationale prompt to turn that list into a structured document.
Ask for the likely pushback on your two or three riskiest decisions specifically, not a generic FAQ.
Review the pushback responses and correct any that overstate your confidence or invent data you don't have.
Ask for a condensed spoken version — talking points, not slide text — for the actual presentation.
Rehearse the talking points once out loud before the meeting; they should sound like you, not like a script.
lessons.prompt:
Help me write a design rationale document for a set of decisions I made on [PROJECT/SCREEN NAME].

My decisions and the real reason behind each (use only what I give you — do not invent user research, data, or justifications I haven't stated):
[LIST: decision 1 + reason, decision 2 + reason, decision 3 + reason, ...]

Write:
1. A short rationale document: one paragraph per decision, framed as [problem/constraint] → [decision] → [outcome or benefit], in plain professional language.
2. For the [NUMBER] riskiest or most likely-to-be-questioned decisions, write the likely stakeholder pushback and a calm, specific response — grounded only in the reasons I gave you, not invented data.
3. A condensed set of spoken talking points (not slide text) I could present from without reading verbatim, covering the same decisions in under 90 seconds.
lessons.explanation: Restricting the document to reasons you actually supply is the core guardrail — a model asked to write a design rationale will otherwise happily invent a plausible-sounding user-research finding to back up a decision, which is exactly the kind of claim that falls apart the moment a stakeholder asks a follow-up question. Requesting pushback and response for the specific riskiest decisions, rather than a generic FAQ, targets rehearsal time where it actually matters instead of padding it with easy questions nobody will ask. Asking for talking points instead of slide text keeps the final presentation from sounding read rather than spoken.
lessons.example:
Decisions: simplified checkout from 4 steps to 2 (reason: brief specified reducing cart abandonment, and moderated usability sessions showed users confused by the third step); moved the price display above the fold (reason: heat-map data showed users scrolling away before finding price).

Expected output: a rationale paragraph for each decision following problem → decision → outcome, a likely pushback like "won't fewer steps mean less opportunity to upsell?" with a grounded response tied only to the stated reasons, and a 90-second spoken version covering both decisions in plain, confident language.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, list the real decisions and reasons behind one project you've designed, generate the rationale document and talking points, and rehearse the talking points out loud once before your next review meeting.
lessons.expectedResult: A short, defensible rationale document plus a condensed spoken version you can present from confidently, with every claim traceable to a reason you actually have.
commonMistakes: Letting the document state a user-research finding or data point you don't actually have to back up a decision.
Writing a rationale for a decision you can't honestly justify, which collapses the first time it's questioned.
Reading the slide-text version aloud in the meeting instead of using the condensed talking points.
Skipping the pushback-and-response step and getting caught flat-footed by the first hard question.
lessons.proTip: Write the rationale document right after you make each decision, not the night before the review — the reasoning is freshest and most specific immediately after you've made the call.

lessons.title: Iterate on a chosen visual direction systematically with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Take one approved mood-board direction through a disciplined refinement loop in ChatGPT so the final visual language stays coherent instead of drifting with each new round.
lessons.goal: Narrow one approved creative direction into a coherent, finished visual language through a controlled refinement loop in ChatGPT, rather than open-ended regeneration.
lessons.whyItMatters: After a direction is chosen, the risk flips — instead of needing variety, you need consistency. Uncontrolled re-prompting after client approval is how a direction that got signed off starts drifting, image by image, until the final asset set doesn't actually match what was approved. ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 supports iterative in-chat editing — asking it to revise or extend an image already in the conversation rather than generating a brand-new one from scratch — which is the exact mechanic that keeps every subsequent generation traceable back to the approved direction, protecting both the visual system and your credibility at the next review.
steps: Pull the exact prompt language and reference images from the approved direction — this becomes your locked style reference, not a rough memory of what people liked.
Identify which specific elements were approved (palette, composition style, texture, mood) versus what's still open (specific subjects, layouts for new assets).
For each new asset needed, change only the subject/scene line and keep every style descriptor identical to the locked reference.

Where possible, request new assets in the same ChatGPT conversation as the originally approved images — GPT Image 2's iterative in-chat editing anchors to what it already generated, which is stronger than reconstructing the style from text alone in a new chat.
If you're starting a new chat or need a stronger anchor, upload an approved reference image and ask ChatGPT to match it exactly for the new asset.
Generate 2-3 options per new asset, then compare each against the locked reference — not against each other — to check for drift.
Flag and regenerate any asset where a style element (palette, texture, mood) has quietly shifted, even if the image looks good on its own.
lessons.prompt:
Locked style reference for this project (do not vary this wording): [PASTE THE APPROVED STYLE BLOCK — palette, composition style, texture/material cues, lighting, mood]

Generate a new asset for: [SPECIFIC NEW SUBJECT/SCENE NEEDED]

Use the locked style reference exactly as written above. Do not introduce a new palette, texture, or mood not present in the reference. Format: [ASPECT RATIO/FORMAT]

If this is the same chat where the approved images were generated, anchor directly to those rather than relying on the text description alone. After generating, list which elements of the locked reference are present in this image, and flag anything that may have drifted.
lessons.explanation: Locking the style-block wording, character for character, is what stops the slow drift that happens when a direction gets re-described slightly differently for each new asset — small paraphrasing changes how GPT Image 2 interprets tone and palette even when the intent seems identical. Running this in the same ChatGPT conversation as the originally approved images gives it a second, stronger anchor beyond the text description, since GPT Image 2's iterative in-chat editing can reference what it already generated rather than reconstructing the style from words alone. Comparing each new generation against the locked reference rather than against the other new images catches drift that would otherwise look fine in isolation but wouldn't survive being placed next to the originally approved board. Asking the model to self-report which elements are present turns the check into a fast scan instead of a full side-by-side every time.
lessons.example:
Approved direction: "flat illustration, muted pastel palette (dusty blue, terracotta, cream), soft rounded shapes, minimal shadows, warm and approachable mood." New asset needed: an icon set for a settings menu, requested in the same ChatGPT thread as the originally approved illustrations.

Expected output: icons that use the exact dusty blue/terracotta/cream palette, soft rounded shapes, and minimal shadow — with the self-report confirming palette and shape language match, and flagging if, say, the shadow rendering came out heavier than the reference, so it can be regenerated before it ships alongside the earlier approved assets.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT, take a direction you've previously had approved (or one from an earlier lesson in this path), lock its exact style-block wording, and generate two new assets using this prompt — ideally in the same chat as the original approved images — checking each against the original reference.
lessons.expectedResult: New assets that visibly belong to the same approved visual system as the original board, with any drifted element caught and regenerated before it reaches a client or final handoff.
commonMistakes: Re-describing the approved style from memory instead of pasting the exact original wording, which introduces drift immediately.
Starting a brand-new ChatGPT chat for every new asset instead of continuing the conversation where the approved images live, losing the stronger in-chat anchor.
Comparing new generations only to each other, missing drift that's only visible against the original approved reference.
Accepting an image that looks good on its own without checking whether it actually matches the locked palette and mood.
lessons.proTip: When a client asks for "just one more variation" late in a project, paste the locked reference back in as a fresh message in the same ChatGPT thread as the original approved images rather than opening a new chat — long-forgotten threads and rewritten descriptions are where style quietly gets reinterpreted.

lessons.title: Build an AI-assisted design process that doesn't erode your craft
lessons.summary: Set explicit rules for where Claude and ChatGPT speed up your process and where they stay hands-off, so AI use compounds your skill instead of quietly replacing your judgment.
lessons.goal: Write a personal (or team) policy — using Claude or ChatGPT to pressure-test it — defining which parts of your design process AI assists and which stay fully manual, based on where speed helps versus where craft and judgment are the actual value you provide.
lessons.whyItMatters: The risk with AI in design isn't that it's bad at any one task — it's that unrestricted use quietly hollows out the skills that make a designer worth hiring: taste, systems thinking, the ability to defend a decision, the instinct for when something is almost right versus actually right. Designers who use tools like Claude and ChatGPT well tend to have a deliberate, explicit line between "AI accelerates this" and "I do this myself, every time" — and that line is worth writing down rather than deciding case by case under deadline pressure.
steps: List every recurring task in your design process, from concept exploration through final handoff.
For each task, honestly assess: does speed matter more here, or does the value come from your own judgment, taste, or hands-on iteration?
Draft a first-pass policy sorting tasks into "AI-assisted" and "manual, always" — expect this to be personal, not a universal rule.
Pressure-test the policy with the reflection prompt below in Claude or ChatGPT, which asks for the specific risk of each AI-assisted category.
Add a review habit for AI-assisted tasks: define what you personally check before accepting the output, not just that you check it.
Revisit the policy after a few months of real use — some tasks will move categories once you've seen where quality actually held up or slipped.
If you work on a team, share the policy and get pushback on it before treating it as settled.
lessons.prompt:
I'm defining where I use AI in my design process and where I keep things fully manual. Here's my task list and my first-pass sorting:

AI-assisted tasks: [LIST]
Manual, always tasks: [LIST]
Reason for each manual task: [WHY — e.g., "this is where client trust in my judgment actually lives" / "this is where I develop taste, not just output"]

Based only on this list (do not add tasks or reasons I haven't given you):
1. For each AI-assisted task, name the specific risk of over-relying on AI there (e.g., visual sameness, losing the ability to defend a decision, missing craft details a client will notice).
2. For each risk, suggest one concrete check I should do before accepting AI output for that task.
3. Flag if any task I put in "AI-assisted," based on my own stated reasons for the manual list, actually looks like it belongs there instead.
lessons.explanation: Restricting the reflection to your own stated list and reasons — rather than letting Claude or ChatGPT propose a generic best-practices policy — is what makes the output a real audit of your process instead of a template that doesn't match how you actually work. Asking for the specific risk of each AI-assisted category, not a general caution, is what makes the pushback useful: "visual sameness" is a different risk with a different check than "losing the ability to defend a decision." The final cross-check — flagging a task that contradicts your own stated manual-task reasoning — is the part most designers skip on their own, since it requires noticing an inconsistency in a list you wrote yourself.
lessons.example:
Task list: AI-assisted — mood board generation (ChatGPT), icon set variations (ChatGPT), first-draft microcopy (Claude). Manual, always — final layout and typography decisions, client rationale conversations, brand mark design. Reason for manual: "this is where clients are paying for my specific judgment, and where I develop taste rather than just approve output."

Expected output: for mood board generation, a flagged risk of visual sameness across projects with a check like "compare this month's ChatGPT boards against last month's before sending"; for microcopy, a flagged risk of losing the specific voice a client hired you for, with a check to read every Claude draft aloud against a real brand-voice example before sending.
lessons.exercise: In Claude or ChatGPT, write your real task list and first-pass sorting for your own design process and run it through this prompt, then commit to one concrete check for each AI-assisted task.
lessons.expectedResult: A written, personal AI-use policy with a specific risk and a specific check attached to each AI-assisted task — something you can actually follow under deadline pressure, not a vague intention to "use AI responsibly."
commonMistakes: Writing the policy once and never revisiting it as your process and the tools both change.
Sorting a task as "AI-assisted" for speed without naming what specifically you're risking by doing so.
Treating the policy as a moral stance rather than a practical craft decision — the point is quality and trust, not resistance to the tools.
Keeping the policy private on a team, so teammates make inconsistent calls about the same task type.
lessons.proTip: Watch for the specific failure mode of visual sameness across projects — if two different clients' ChatGPT-generated concept boards start looking interchangeable, that's the clearest signal a task has drifted from "assisted" to "outsourced," and it's worth moving back toward manual.

lessons.title: Turn client inquiries into booking replies with Claude
lessons.summary: Reply to a new inquiry with a warm, specific message that answers the client's real question and moves them toward booking, without it reading like a copy-paste template.
lessons.goal: Draft a personalized inquiry reply that answers the client's actual question and includes one clear next step toward booking, within minutes of receiving the message.
lessons.whyItMatters: The first reply is often the deciding factor in whether an inquiry becomes a booking — a slow, generic response loses leads to photographers who reply faster and warmer. Photographers get the same handful of inquiry types repeatedly (availability, pricing, style fit), which makes this an ideal task to speed up without it reading as automated, as long as the reply actually engages with what the specific person asked.
steps: Paste the client's inquiry message exactly as received.
Note your real availability, relevant package info, and anything specific to reference (their date, venue, occasion) that you already know.
Use the reply prompt, which requires referencing at least one specific detail from their message.
Review the draft for tone — warm and personal, not a form letter.
Include one clear, low-friction next step (a call, a questionnaire, confirming a date) rather than several asks at once.
Send from your own email or inquiry system.
lessons.prompt:
Write a reply to this client inquiry.

Client's message:
[PASTE INQUIRY EXACTLY AS RECEIVED]

My real details to include: [AVAILABILITY FOR THEIR DATE / RELEVANT PACKAGE NAME AND WHAT IT INCLUDES / ANYTHING SPECIFIC ABOUT THEIR EVENT OR REQUEST I ALREADY KNOW]

Rules:
- Reference at least one specific detail from their message (their date, venue, occasion, or stated concern) — do not write a generic reply.
- Directly answer whatever they actually asked (availability, pricing, style) before adding anything else.
- Warm, professional tone, no pressure language ("spots are filling fast").
- End with exactly one clear next step (e.g., a specific question, a link to book a call, or confirming the date).
- Do not invent pricing, availability, or package details I haven't given you — use a placeholder like [CONFIRM] if something is missing.
lessons.explanation: Requiring a specific reference from the client's own message is what makes the reply feel personally read rather than templated, and it's the single biggest lever for a fast, warm response that actually gets a reply back. Capping the message to one clear next step keeps a hesitant inquiry from stalling out on too many choices, and banning invented pricing or availability keeps you from accidentally quoting something you'd have to walk back later. Answering their actual question first, before any other content, respects that most inquiries are genuinely just trying to find out one or two things.
lessons.example:
Inquiry: "Hi, are you available for a wedding on June 14th at Riverside Gardens? What packages do you offer?"

Expected output: a reply that opens by confirming (or checking) availability for June 14th specifically, mentions Riverside Gardens by name, briefly outlines the relevant package(s) with real details supplied, and closes with one next step — such as offering a 15-minute call to talk through coverage needs — rather than listing every package and every possible add-on at once.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, use a real recent inquiry (or a practice one) to draft a reply with this prompt, then send it after your own review.
lessons.expectedResult: A specific, warm reply that answers the client's actual question and ends with one clear next step, sent the same day the inquiry arrives.
commonMistakes: Sending a fully generic reply that doesn't reference anything specific from the client's message.
Listing every package and add-on instead of answering what was actually asked.
Using urgency language ("booking fast for this season") that can read as pressure on a first reply.
Letting the draft quote pricing or availability you haven't actually confirmed.
lessons.proTip: Keep a short list of your 3-4 most common inquiry types and their real answers (availability process, starting price, typical turnaround) so filling in the prompt takes seconds even on a busy day.

lessons.title: Prepare for a shoot: build a shot list and mood board with Claude and ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn a client's must-have shots and vibe words into an organized shot list with Claude, plus a quick visual mood board in ChatGPT you can review with the client before shoot day.
lessons.goal: Produce an organized, time-sequenced shot list with Claude and a supporting mood board in ChatGPT from a client's raw notes, ready to review before the shoot.
lessons.whyItMatters: Shoot day moves fast, and the shots you forget to plan for are the ones you don't get back — the specific family combination, the ring-detail shot, the getting-ready moment a client assumed was obvious. Claude turns scattered client notes and your own experience into a checklist you can actually run through on location, and a quick ChatGPT-generated mood board gets everyone (client, second shooter, assistant) aligned on the visual goal before anyone shows up.
steps: Gather the client's must-have shots, any people/groupings they specified, the schedule/timeline, and any style references they mentioned.
Use the shot-list prompt in Claude to organize everything into a time-sequenced, checkable list.
Flag anything ambiguous — an unclear grouping, a missing timeline slot — rather than guessing at it.
Separately, pull 2-3 vibe words or reference images the client gave you and generate a short mood board in ChatGPT using GPT Image 2, to confirm the visual direction matches what they meant.
Share both the shot list and the mood board with the client for a quick yes/no before shoot day.
Print or save the shot list somewhere accessible without unlocking a phone mid-shoot.
lessons.prompt:
Build a time-sequenced shot list for a [EVENT/SESSION TYPE] on [DATE], using only the details below. Flag anything unclear instead of guessing.

Schedule/timeline: [PASTE TIMELINE, e.g., "getting ready 1pm, ceremony 3pm, reception 6pm"]
Must-have shots the client mentioned: [LIST]
Key people/groupings needed: [LIST, e.g., "bride with each grandparent individually, full wedding party, immediate family only"]
Location notes: [ANY KNOWN DETAILS]

Organize the shot list by time block (e.g., "Getting Ready," "Ceremony," "Formals," "Reception"), as a checkable list under each block. For any grouping or moment that's ambiguous or missing a time slot, add it to a separate "Confirm with client" list instead of guessing where it fits.
lessons.explanation: Organizing by time block rather than as one flat list is what makes a shot list actually usable on location — you can glance at the current block instead of scanning fifty lines under time pressure. Routing anything ambiguous into a separate "Confirm with client" list, instead of letting Claude guess at a grouping or slot, is the guardrail that prevents a missed must-have shot from being discovered only after the event is over. Pairing the shot list with a quick ChatGPT mood board (built the same way as the concept-exploration lesson in this path) closes a common gap: a client's must-have list tells you what to shoot, but the mood board confirms how it should feel, since words like "candid" or "romantic" can mean very differently to different clients.
lessons.example:
Session: a wedding, timeline getting ready 1pm / ceremony 3pm / reception 6pm. Must-have shots: "detail shot of the rings," "first look," "bride with each grandparent." Groupings: "immediate family only," "full wedding party." Location: unfamiliar venue, no site visit done.

Expected output: a list organized under Getting Ready, Ceremony, Formals, and Reception headers with each must-have shot placed in the right block, plus a "Confirm with client" list flagging that "bride with each grandparent" needs a headcount and that formals timing at an unfamiliar venue may need a buffer — rather than silently assuming a duration.
lessons.exercise: In Claude, build a shot list for an upcoming (or recent) session using this prompt, and separately generate a 3-4 image mood board in ChatGPT using the client's own vibe words, then share both with the client.
lessons.expectedResult: A time-blocked, checkable shot list with any ambiguous request flagged for confirmation, plus a small mood board that verifies the visual direction with the client before the shoot.
commonMistakes: Letting Claude guess at an ambiguous grouping instead of flagging it for confirmation.
Building the shot list but skipping the ChatGPT mood-board check, then discovering on shoot day that "candid" meant something different to the client.
Keeping the shot list only on a phone that becomes inaccessible mid-shoot.
Not leaving buffer time between blocks at an unfamiliar venue, which the flagged-ambiguity step is meant to catch.
lessons.proTip: Reuse the same time-block headers across every session type you shoot — the consistency makes it faster to build each new list and easier to train a second shooter or assistant on how you work.

lessons.title: Write clear pricing and package descriptions with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn your actual pricing structure into package descriptions that are easy to compare and don't oversell what's included.
lessons.goal: Produce clear, comparable package descriptions for your pricing page or PDF guide, built strictly from your real pricing and inclusions.
lessons.whyItMatters: Confusing pricing pages cost photographers bookings two ways — clients who can't tell what's actually included message with basic questions instead of booking, and clients who feel misled after the fact leave bad reviews. Clear, honest package copy that's easy to compare side by side reduces both problems, but only if the copy is constrained to your real numbers and inclusions rather than writing persuasive-sounding language that implies more than what's actually offered.
steps: List your actual packages: name, price, exact inclusions (hours, number of images, prints, delivery time), and what's explicitly NOT included.
Use the pricing-copy prompt, which bans adding any inclusion you didn't list.
Ask for a comparison-friendly format — consistent structure across all packages — so clients can scan and compare easily.
Review each package description against your actual contract terms — nothing implied should exceed what you'd actually deliver.
Ask for a short "which package is right for you" guide based only on the differences you listed.
Publish only after checking that prices and inclusions are current.
lessons.prompt:
Write pricing package descriptions for my photography business using only the details below. Do not add any inclusion, feature, or benefit I haven't listed, and do not imply more service than what's stated.

Packages:
[FOR EACH PACKAGE: name, price, hours of coverage, number of edited images delivered, delivery timeframe, prints/albums included if any, what's explicitly NOT included]

Write:
1. A short, comparison-friendly description for each package (consistent structure across all of them: headline, price, bullet list of inclusions, one line on who it fits).
2. A brief "Which package is right for you" guide based only on the actual differences between the packages listed above (coverage length, deliverables) — not invented lifestyle framing.

Tone: confident and clear, no pressure language, no vague value claims ("best value," "most popular") unless I've told you which one actually sells best.
lessons.explanation: Banning added inclusions is the core guardrail here — a model asked to write persuasive package copy will otherwise round up ("unlimited edits," "premium album included") in ways that create a real dispute the first time a client checks their contract against the website. Requiring a consistent structure across every package is what makes them scannable and comparable, which is exactly the decision-making aid confused shoppers need before they'll message with a question instead of book. Restricting value claims like "most popular" to only what you've actually told it keeps the copy honest instead of using generic sales language that reads as untrustworthy the moment a client senses it isn't true.
lessons.example:
Packages: "Essential — $1,200, 4 hours coverage, 100 edited images, delivered in 4 weeks, no prints"; "Signature — $2,400, 8 hours coverage, 300 edited images, delivered in 3 weeks, one 10x10 album included."

Expected output: two descriptions in identical structure (headline, price, bulleted inclusions, one-line fit statement) with nothing added beyond hours, image count, delivery time, and the album — and a "which is right for you" guide framed around actual coverage length and deliverables, not an invented claim like "perfect for large weddings" unless that was part of what was given.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, list your real packages and generate the comparison-friendly descriptions and guide with this prompt, then check every line against your actual contract terms before publishing.
lessons.expectedResult: Clear, consistently structured package descriptions and a short selection guide that a client could use to choose confidently without messaging a basic clarifying question first.
commonMistakes: Letting the draft imply an inclusion (like unlimited revisions) that isn't actually part of the package.
Using inconsistent structure between packages, making them harder to compare at a glance.
Adding a vague value claim ("best value") without any real basis for it.
Publishing before checking that the prices and inclusions are still current.
lessons.proTip: Update the packages list the moment a real price or inclusion changes, and regenerate from that same prompt — it keeps your website, PDF guide, and inquiry replies all quoting the same numbers.

lessons.title: Write website copy and social captions that market your photography with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn your actual work and voice into homepage copy and a batch of social captions that sound like you, not like a stock template.
lessons.goal: Produce homepage/about copy and a batch of social captions for recent work, grounded in your real experience and voice rather than generic photographer marketing language.
lessons.whyItMatters: Photography marketing copy is easy to write badly — every studio's homepage claims to "capture your story" and "tell it through timeless images," which means none of them say anything a potential client actually remembers. Grounding the copy in your specific experience, specialty, and real client outcomes is what makes it sound like a real business instead of a template, and a repeatable caption process keeps you posting consistently instead of only when inspiration strikes.
steps: Write down your real specifics: years shooting, specialty, what clients actually say about working with you, and one or two real moments or outcomes you're proud of.
Use the website-copy prompt to draft homepage/about copy from those specifics, banning the generic phrases you want to avoid.
Separately, gather 4-6 recent images or sessions with one factual note each (what/where/who, only what you can share publicly).
Use the caption prompt to generate a batch of platform-appropriate captions from those notes in one pass.
Review every caption for client privacy — remove any identifying detail you don't have permission to share publicly.
Schedule the batch across the week rather than posting it all at once.
lessons.prompt:
Write website homepage/about copy for my photography business using only the specifics below. Avoid generic photography marketing phrases like "capture your story," "timeless images," or "tell your love story" — write something specific to me instead.

My specifics: [YEARS SHOOTING, SPECIALTY (e.g., wedding, family, product), WHAT CLIENTS ACTUALLY SAY ABOUT WORKING WITH ME, ONE OR TWO REAL MOMENTS/OUTCOMES I'M PROUD OF, MY ACTUAL SHOOTING STYLE IN MY OWN WORDS]

Write:
1. A homepage hero section (headline + 2-3 sentence subhead)
2. A short About section (100-150 words) in first person
3. Then, using these recent session notes: [FOR EACH: what/where/who, only shareable facts], write 4-6 social captions (Instagram-length, my voice, one specific detail from each session's notes, one soft call to action per caption, varied — not the same structure repeated).

Do not invent client quotes, testimonials, or session details I haven't given you.
lessons.explanation: Naming the exact clichés to avoid ("capture your story," "timeless images") is more effective than a general "be specific" instruction, because those are precisely the phrases a model defaults to when asked for photography marketing copy without other constraints. Requiring real specifics — actual client feedback, a real remembered moment — is what gives the copy something distinctive to say instead of a polished restatement of what every competitor's site already says. Generating a batch of captions from real session notes in one pass, with a rule against repeating the same structure, is what keeps a week of posts from reading like the same caption with the nouns swapped.
lessons.example:
Specifics: 6 years shooting, specialty in documentary-style family sessions, clients often say they forgot the camera was even there, proud moment: a grandmother seeing her whole family together in one frame for the first time in a decade.

Expected output: a homepage headline and subhead built around the documentary, unposed style and that specific kind of moment rather than "capturing your story," an About section written in first person referencing the real six-year specialty, and captions for recent sessions that each reference one true detail (a specific location, a specific interaction) instead of a repeated generic template.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, write your real specifics and 4-6 recent session notes, then generate the homepage copy and caption batch with this prompt, removing any detail you don't have permission to share.
lessons.expectedResult: Homepage/about copy that reads as specific to your business rather than interchangeable with any other photographer's site, plus a week's worth of varied, specific social captions ready to schedule.
commonMistakes: Letting generic phrases like "capture your story" slip through unedited because they sound fine on a first read.
Posting a client-identifying detail (a full name, an address, a private family event) without permission.
Generating all captions with the same opening structure, making the batch feel repetitive even though the content differs.
Skipping real specifics and letting the copy default to generic professional language that could describe any photographer.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running note of real client comments and small standout moments from every session — even one line — so you always have fresh, specific material instead of reaching for the same two anecdotes every time you write copy.

lessons.title: Write client gallery delivery emails and print upsells with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn gallery delivery into a warm, well-timed email plus an honest upsell offer for prints or albums, without pressure tactics that undercut the moment.
lessons.goal: Draft a gallery delivery email and a follow-up upsell message for prints/albums that feels like part of the experience, not a separate sales pitch.
lessons.whyItMatters: Gallery delivery is the emotional peak of the client relationship, and also the highest-leverage moment for print and album sales, which carry far better margins than digital-only packages. Photographers who treat delivery as just an email with a link leave that revenue on the table; photographers who turn every delivery into a hard sell damage the goodwill they just earned. A well-timed, honest two-part message — the delivery, then a separate low-pressure upsell — gets both right.
steps: Note the session specifics: client name, session type, gallery link, delivery timeframe you promised, and anything memorable from the session worth referencing.
Use the delivery-email prompt to draft the gallery delivery message on its own, focused purely on the delivery experience.
List your actual print/album products and prices for the upsell portion — don't let the draft invent products you don't offer.
Use the upsell portion of the prompt to draft a separate follow-up message, meant to send a few days later, offering prints without pressure language.
Review both for tone — the delivery email should feel personal and celebratory; the upsell should feel like a helpful option, not a pitch.
Schedule the upsell to send a few days after delivery, once the client has had time to view the gallery.
lessons.prompt:
Write two separate client messages for a photography session.

Session details: [CLIENT NAME, SESSION TYPE, ONE SPECIFIC MEMORABLE MOMENT FROM THE SESSION, GALLERY LINK, ANY DELIVERY-TIMEFRAME PROMISE I MADE]

Message 1 — Gallery delivery email: warm, personal, references the specific memorable moment, includes the gallery link, states how long the gallery stays live if applicable, under 150 words. No sales content in this message.

Message 2 — Print/album upsell (a separate follow-up, to send a few days later): using only these real products and prices: [LIST YOUR ACTUAL PRINTS/ALBUMS AND PRICES], write a short, low-pressure message offering these as an option, framed around preserving/displaying the images rather than urgency or scarcity language. One clear next step (a link or a reply prompt), no countdown or "limited time" framing unless I've told you there's a real deadline.

Do not invent products, prices, or a deadline I haven't given you.
lessons.explanation: Keeping the delivery email free of any sales content is deliberate — mixing an upsell into the moment a client first sees their images undercuts the emotional response that's actually driving the sale, so the prompt separates the two by design, not just by timing. Framing the upsell around preserving and displaying the images, rather than urgency, matches how people actually decide to buy prints: as a considered choice about a memory they already value, not a reaction to a countdown. Banning invented products, prices, or deadlines keeps the upsell honest about what you actually offer, since an invented "limited time" claim is the fastest way to damage trust right after a client's best moment with you.
lessons.example:
Session: the Alvarez family, fall mini session, memorable moment was the youngest child laughing uncontrollably during a leaf-throwing shot, gallery link included, promised 2-week delivery, actual products: an 8x10 matte print ($45), a 20-page linen album ($350).

Expected output: a delivery email opening with something like "I'm so glad I get to share these with you — that leaf-throwing shot of [child's name] mid-laugh is one of my favorites from the whole fall season," with the gallery link and no pricing mentioned; a separate, later message offering the print and album at their real prices, framed around having something to actually hang or hold rather than urgency.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, use real (or recent) session details and your actual print/album pricing to draft both messages with this prompt, and schedule the upsell to send a few days after delivery.
lessons.expectedResult: A warm, sales-free delivery email and a separate, honest, low-pressure upsell message with your real products and prices, sent on a two-step timeline rather than combined into one email.
commonMistakes: Combining the delivery and the upsell into a single email, which undercuts the emotional moment with a pitch.
Using urgency or countdown language for an upsell with no real deadline behind it.
Letting the draft invent a product or price you don't actually offer.
Sending the upsell too soon, before the client has had time to view and react to the gallery.
lessons.proTip: Track which upsell offers actually convert by session type — the framing that works for a wedding album is rarely the one that works for a family mini session print, and your own data will tell you faster than a guess.

lessons.title: Build a season-proof marketing routine with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn your booking calendar's seasonal peaks and slow stretches into a standing marketing routine that keeps leads coming in year-round instead of only during your busy season.
lessons.goal: Design a documented, repeatable marketing routine mapped to your actual seasonal booking pattern, so slow months get deliberate marketing instead of being left to chance.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most photography niches are seasonal — wedding season, back-to-school family sessions, holiday minis — and the natural trap is marketing hardest when you're already busiest and going quiet exactly when you need new bookings most. A documented routine tied to your real calendar, not a generic content-calendar template, is what keeps outreach, content, and past-client re-engagement happening in your slow months, when it actually moves revenue.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a rough sense of your last 12 months of bookings by month, and know which platforms (Instagram, email list, referral partners) you actually use regularly.
steps: Map your real booking pattern across the year: peak months, slow months, and any recurring seasonal offer you run (minis, holiday packages).
For each slow-season stretch, identify the actual goal: fill the calendar, launch a new offer, re-engage past clients, or build a content backlog for peak season.
Use the routine-building prompt to turn your calendar and goals into a month-by-month marketing routine.
Ask for the routine broken into recurring weekly/monthly actions, not one-off ideas, so it survives becoming a habit rather than a list you write once and forget.
Identify which actions from earlier in this path (inquiry replies, package copy, social captions, gallery upsells) plug into which month of the routine.
Set one calendar reminder per recurring action rather than relying on memory.
Review actual booking results against the routine after one full cycle and adjust which months need more effort.
lessons.prompt:
Help me build a season-proof marketing routine for my photography business, using only the details below — do not invent a niche, offer, or platform I haven't mentioned.

My niche: [e.g., wedding / family / newborn / product photography]
Peak booking months: [LIST]
Slow months: [LIST]
Recurring seasonal offers I run (if any): [LIST, e.g., "fall mini sessions," "holiday card sessions"]
Platforms I actually use for marketing: [LIST, e.g., Instagram, a mailing list, referral partners]
Past-client list size (roughly): [NUMBER OR "not tracked"]

Build a month-by-month routine covering the full year with:
1. For each slow month: one clear marketing goal (fill calendar / launch offer / re-engage past clients / build content backlog) and 2-3 recurring weekly or monthly actions to support it, using only the platforms I listed.
2. For each peak month: what to prepare in advance (content, templates, offer copy) so peak-season execution doesn't require new creative thinking under deadline pressure.
3. A short section noting which actions should be recurring habits versus one-time setup tasks.

Keep it realistic for a solo or small photography business — no more than a few hours per week of marketing effort total.
lessons.explanation: Mapping the routine to your actual peak and slow months, rather than a generic 12-month content calendar, is what makes the plan usable — a routine that tells you to "post consistently year-round" ignores that your slow-season marketing goal (fill the calendar) is fundamentally different from your peak-season need (prepare content in advance so you're not writing captions during a wedding weekend). Restricting the routine to platforms you actually use prevents a plan that quietly assumes a TikTok strategy you have no intention of running. Separating recurring habits from one-time setup tasks is what keeps the routine alive after the first month, since habits need a standing reminder while setup tasks just need to get done once.
lessons.example:
Niche: wedding photography. Peak months: May-October. Slow months: January-March. Recurring offer: none currently. Platforms: Instagram and an email list of past clients (about 150 people).

Expected output: for January-March, a goal of "re-engage past clients and fill early-year gaps," with recurring actions like a monthly email to the past-client list featuring one story from a recent wedding plus a referral prompt, and a weekly Instagram post pulled from a backlog of unpublished peak-season images; for May-October, a note to prewrite caption templates and gallery-delivery copy in April, before the season's pace makes that impossible; and a clear split marking the email list and referral prompt as recurring habits versus the April prep work as a one-time seasonal task.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, map your real booking pattern and platforms, generate the routine with this prompt, and set calendar reminders for each recurring action before the season changes.
lessons.expectedResult: A realistic, month-by-month marketing routine tied to your actual calendar, with slow months getting a deliberate goal and recurring actions instead of no marketing at all, and peak months protected by advance preparation.
commonMistakes: Building a generic 12-month content calendar that ignores your actual seasonal booking pattern.
Planning a routine on platforms you don't actually use, so it quietly gets abandoned.
Not distinguishing recurring habits from one-time tasks, so the whole routine gets treated as a to-do list that's "done" once completed.
Reviewing the routine only when a slow month is already underway instead of before it starts.
lessons.proTip: Build your peak-season content backlog during your slowest month, not your second-slowest — that's the only time you'll realistically have both the material and the time to prepare it properly.
